section_summary: This closing section contains public protests and a petition urging the United States to stop exports of arms, lead, oil, scrap iron, and other war materials to Japan during the Sino-Japanese War. State Department replies explain that the Neutrality Act could embargo arms only after a presidential proclamation of war—which would affect China as well as Japan—and did not authorize restrictions on commodities such as lead. The section also includes guidance on American property-damage claims against Japan and a cross-reference to a Chinese study of Japan’s ability to finance war-material purchases.

subfiles.title: Concluding page of Mrs. W. D. Boone’s protest concerning Japan
subfiles.about: The fragment argues that delayed American action emboldens Japan to continue destruction and killing.
subfiles.summary: This is the closing page of a letter that began before the supplied section. Although much of the OCR is illegible, the writer plainly condemns deliberate delay, warns that it encourages Japan, and urges stronger action before signing as Mrs. W. D. Boone.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mrs. W. D. Boone
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains the legal limits on restricting exports to Japan and provides procedures for American claims arising from Japanese military action in China.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that a presidential finding of war under the Neutrality Act would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan, while no statutory authority existed to stop them without such a proclamation or to restrict non-arms commodities. It reports arms-export licenses since July 1, 1937, valued at $14,218,523.21 for China and $10,793,865.38 for Japan, and reiterates the government’s condemnation of civilian bombing. It also explains how American nationals or missionary organizations may submit claims for Japanese-caused losses through American diplomatic and consular offices or directly to the Department.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on language for replying about claims against Japan
subfiles.from: B. M. English, Office of the Legal Adviser
subfiles.about: The memorandum supplies proposed language concerning Japanese responsibility for American property losses and the filing of claims.
subfiles.summary: The Legal Adviser’s office notes that Miss Christenson had referred Mrs. Boone’s letter for consideration. It recommends advising the writer that the United States had notified Japan it would seek compensation where liability existed under international law. The proposed text directs claimants to use the Department’s prepared guidance and to file in China through the nearest American diplomatic or consular office, or from the United States directly with the Department.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to booklet on Japan’s ability to finance war-material purchases
subfiles.about: The sheet redirects researchers to file 894.51/599 for a Chinese Council for Economic Research booklet on Japan’s war-purchasing finances.
subfiles.summary: This document-file note points to file 894.51/599. The referenced item is a booklet prepared by the Chinese Council for Economic Research concerning Japan’s ability to finance purchases of war materials; its title is not preserved in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding a petition on the Japanese invasion of China
subfiles.about: The sender forwards a petition concerning the Japanese invasion of China for the President’s serious consideration.
subfiles.summary: The badly degraded letter addresses President Roosevelt and encloses a petition about the Japanese invasion of China. The date and sender are corroborated by the State Department’s subsequent reply, which identifies an October 8 letter from Mr. Haskell enclosing the petition.

subfiles.title: Petition to the President on the Japanese invasion of China
subfiles.from: W. W. Haskell and other petitioners, principally from the West Plains, Missouri, area
subfiles.about: The petition asks the President to use every practical means to end American trade that supports Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: The petition accuses Japan of violating the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact and condemns the bombing of Chinese cities and civilians. It argues that American aircraft, bombs, shells, scrap iron, oil, trucks, and other materials are sustaining Japanese aggression and allowing American interests to profit from Chinese suffering. Invoking Roosevelt’s Good Neighbor principle, the signers request direct or indirect action to end the traffic, followed by two pages of mostly handwritten signatures and addresses.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to W. W. Haskell regarding the petition
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the petition and explains why the President had not invoked the Neutrality Act against arms exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply acknowledges Haskell’s October 8 petition, referred by the White House, and explains that a presidential proclamation would embargo arms to China as well as Japan. It says the President concluded that invoking the law would not serve the broad interests of the United States and that the act did not cover non-arms commodities. The letter reports licenses since July 1, 1937, of $14,265,554.11 for China and $10,793,865.38 for Japan and repeats the government’s condemnation of civilian bombing.

subfiles.title: Alfred C. Schmitt’s protest against sales of war materials to Japan
subfiles.about: Schmitt protests the sale of American war materials and lead to Japan for use against the Chinese people.
subfiles.summary: Schmitt contrasts American Christian missionary work in China and Japan with the government’s permission for exports that support Japan’s war. Referring to a newspaper photograph of a Japanese ship loading American lead for bullets, he asks the government to stop what he calls a wicked and inhuman traffic. He argues that Americans should not profit from the attempted destruction of the Chinese people.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Alfred C. Schmitt
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains that existing neutrality legislation did not authorize the President or Secretary of State to prohibit exports of lead to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply explains that a proclamation under the Neutrality Act would bar arms exports to both China and Japan, while no such prohibition could be imposed without it. It emphasizes that the act covered only enumerated arms, ammunition, and implements of war and specifically notes that lead was not included, leaving no statutory authority to prohibit its export. The letter also reports arms-export licenses of $14,265,554.11 for China and $10,793,865.38 for Japan since July 1, 1937.
